Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:67: And in the Zohar (Parashat Mishpatim, page 122a), in these words: we have learned, Israel are called "holy," and because they are holy, it is forbidden for people to call their fellow by a disgraceful name, and not to give a nickname to one's fellow, and its punishment is great, all the more so with other words. Rabbi Yosi said, whoever calls his fellow by a name that is not in him, and shames him with it, is caught by what is not in him - for Rabbi Chiya said in the name of Rabbi Chizkiyah, whoever calls his fellow "wicked" brings him down to Gehinnom, and brings down his own worlds [i.e., harms himself], except when the Torah's own strong ones are involved, for a person is permitted to call them wicked - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:68: And after we have spoken of the parts of slander as found in the books, we must explain the punishment of one who accepts the evil report. In Tractate Pesachim (118a), Rav Sheshet said in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, whoever speaks slander, whoever accepts slander, and whoever testifies falsely against his fellow, deserves to be cast to the dogs, as it is said (Exodus 22:30), "you shall cast it to the dogs," and right after it, "you shall not accept a false report" - to this point. And in the Mechilta they said, "keep far from a false matter" (Exodus 23:7) - this is a warning to those who accept slander.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:69: Further, they said in Pesachim (87b), why did Jeroboam merit to be counted among the kings of Israel and Judah? Because he did not accept slander, and so on - see there. And we also find that because David accepted slander from Ziba concerning Mephibosheth, the kingdom of the house of David was divided, as we read in Tractate Shabbat (56b): they said, of blessed memory, Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, at the time David said to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:30), "you and Ziba shall divide the field," a heavenly voice went out and said, Rehoboam and Jeroboam shall divide the kingdom. And if in a matter of recognizable facts, [David's error in] considering the matter believable caused such a great breach through the acceptance of slander, all the more so must a person distance himself and stop his ears from hearing the slander spoken every day about innocent people.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:70: And one who accepts slander and shows in his soul that he agrees with the speaker and believes the words in front of people, is as though he spoke it, for he assists in the evil and causes disgrace to his fellow - for when the informer sees the face of the listener frowning, he ceases his words, but if he sees that the listener heeds him, he will not withhold his lies. And to this we were warned, "you shall not accept a false report" - that we not believe in our hearts a slanderous report, holding in our thoughts that those words are true, to disgrace the one about whom they are said, Heaven forfend.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:71: And in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Zuta, chapter 7), they said, of blessed memory: it is said of Jeroboam ben Yoash that he showed honor to prophets - and what the Holy One, blessed be He, did not give into the hand of Joshua son of Nun and into the hand of David king of Israel, He gave into his hand, as it is said (2 Kings 14:25), "he restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah." Similarly you say (2 Kings 14:26), "for the LORD saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter, for there was none shut up or left at large, nor any helper for Israel; and the LORD had not said He would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven" - and what merit did Jeroboam have in this matter, was he not an idol worshipper? Rather, it was because he did not accept slander against the prophet Amos, as it is said (Amos 7:10), "then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos has conspired against you," and so on, "thus says Amos, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be exiled from its land" - he immediately rebuked him and expelled him with a reproof, saying, Heaven forfend, that righteous man did not prophesy this prophecy of his own accord, but from Heaven. At that hour the Holy One, blessed be He, said, a generation that worships idols, the head of the generation worships idols, yet did not accept slander - the land that I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, to your seed I shall give it, I shall give into his hand, and he restored the border of Israel - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:72: And further, among the things that blemish the covenant of the tongue, related to the matter of slander, is that one must be careful not to curse his fellow by the Name - even without mentioning the LORD, only in a foreign language, it is forbidden and transgresses a negative commandment - and even bringing forth a curse from his mouth unintentionally is unfitting, for a covenant is made with the lips (Mo'ed Katan 18a), and how many have been punished for this, as it is said in the Talmud several times (ibid.), "it was like an error that goes out from before a ruler."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:73: And he says in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach, page 175a), concerning the death of Rachel, that our father Jacob, peace be upon him, caused her death by cursing without intent, in these words: Rabbi Yosi said, it is written (Proverbs 26:2), "a causeless curse shall not [lo] come" - and they established it as "lo" with a vav [meaning "to him," implying it does come, but to the curser]. And if it is a righteous person's curse, even if he did not intend it, once it emerges from his mouth, that evil inclination takes it and accuses with it at a time of danger. Jacob said (Genesis 31:32), "with whomever you find your gods, he shall not live" - and although he did not know, that Satan, who is always found among people, took that word. And therefore we have learned, a person should never open his mouth to Satan, because he takes that word and accuses with it above and below - all the more so a word of a sage or a word of a righteous person - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:74: And so they said, of blessed memory, in Tractate Makkot (11a): Rabbi Abahu said, the curse of a sage, even if for no reason, comes to pass - from where do we know this? From Eli, who said to Samuel (1 Samuel 3:17), "so may God do to you, and more also, if you hide a word from me" - and although it is written, "and Samuel told him all the words and hid nothing from him," it is written (ibid. 8:3), "and his sons did not walk in his ways." And they brought another proof there, which we shall not copy, so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:75: And of this kind is that one should not curse someone who does not hear him, as the Targum explains on (Exodus 19:14, actually Leviticus 19:14) "you shall not curse the deaf" - do not curse one who does not hear. And so they said in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim, page 85a): come and see, whoever curses his fellow while he is present and shames him is as though he shed his blood, and this has been established. But this verse speaks of one who curses someone not with him, and that word curses him - and there is no single word that emerges from his mouth that has no voice, and that voice ascends above, and how many recorders join with that voice, until it ascends and arouses the place of the great abyss, as they have established, and how many are aroused against that person - woe to whoever brings forth an evil word from his mouth, and this has been established - to this point. And the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Love of God, chapter 6), how despicable are the common people in this, bringing forth curses and blasphemies from their mouths.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:76: Further, one should be careful not to curse himself in anger - for in the fourth palace of the palaces of the husks there are powers called "cursers of the day," who take that curse a person cursed himself with and fulfill it, Heaven forfend (Parashat Pekudei, page 266a). And this is one of the three things that cause harm to oneself, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, page 14b, and also page 8b), that because David said (2 Samuel 12:5), "the man who did this deserves death," and so on, Dumah seized him, and had the Holy One, blessed be He, not assisted him, he would have fallen into the hand of Dumah, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 94:17), "unless the LORD had been my help, my soul would have soon dwelt in Dumah [silence/the netherworld]."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:77: And concerning something similar, they said, of blessed memory, that a person should never open his mouth to Satan, as we read in the chapter "Mi SheMeto" (Berachot 19a), in these words: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, and so it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosi, a person should never open his mouth to Satan. And Rav Yosef said, what is the verse? As it is said (Isaiah 1:9), "we would have been almost like Sodom" - what did the prophet answer him? (ibid. 1:10), "hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom." And it says further there, before this, that for this reason the mourner should not say, in acknowledging divine judgment, "Master of the universe, I have sinned much before You and You have not exacted from me one part in a thousand." And likewise it is fitting that a man not curse his wife, for the male is half the body, and the two of them together are one complete person - and if he curses her he is found cursing himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:78: And it appears to me that the warning for all these aspects is from the verse (Exodus 23:13), "and make no mention of the name of other gods" - for all the blemishes of the tongue are from the side of the external force, which is "other gods." And so King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 34:14), "guard your tongue from evil" - the intent being that all things that have a grasp on "ra" [evil], which is Samael - and when he guards his tongue, he shall merit life and good, as it says (Psalms 34:13), "who is the man who desires life, who loves days," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:79: And with this the chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:1: After we have spoken, in the previous chapters, of the matter of the four groups that do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah, it remains for us to explain, in this chapter, the matter of vows and oaths that depend on the tongue, and likewise all the other things that blemish speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:2: Concerning the matter of oaths, Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor (part 1, letter 38), in these words: those who swear by the blessed Name mean to say that just as He, blessed be He, is true, so their words are true, whether past or future - and one who swears falsely is like one who denies the truth of the Name. And if a person swears by the head of a king of flesh and blood and does not fulfill his word, he is deserving of death, since he has disgraced the king's honor - and if this is fitting to do to one who swears by a king of flesh and blood, who comes from a putrid drop and shall eventually die, all the more so must a person guard his mouth and tongue lest it cause him to make his flesh sin by swearing falsely by the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who lives and endures forever. And we already know what happened to the children of Israel because they swore publicly concerning the matter of the concubine at Gibeah, and likewise the famine the Name brought upon the land because of Saul and his house, who transgressed the oath of the princes who swore to the Gibeonites (Bamidbar Rabbah 5:3). And we see that no explicit punishment is written in the warnings of the Ten Commandments except for idolatry and "you shall not take [the Name in vain]" - and yet people are so accustomed to this matter that some transgress it a hundred times a day without receiving any benefit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:3: And because people are not expert in the severity of an oath and its great weight, they come to blind their eyes and swear falsely - therefore our Rabbis instituted that the court, in every era, inform the one taking the oath of the severity of the oath and its law, in language he understands, in order to open his ear, so that perhaps he fear and withdraw from the oath - as we read in Tractate Shevuot (38b): our Rabbis taught, the oath of judges is also stated in its own language - they say to him, know that the whole world trembled at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, said (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God in vain" - and for all the transgressions in the Torah, punishment is exacted from him alone, but here, from him and from his family, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 5:5), "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" - and "his flesh" refers only to his relative, as it is said (Isaiah 58:7), "and do not hide yourself from your own flesh." And for all the transgressions in the Torah, punishment is exacted from him alone, but here, from him and from the whole world, as it is said (Hosea 4:2), "swearing falsely," and it is written (ibid. 4:3), "therefore the land mourns." And for all the transgressions in the Torah, if he has merit, they suspend [punishment] for two or three generations, but here punishment is exacted immediately, as it is said (Zechariah 5:4), "I have sent it forth, says the LORD, and it shall enter the house of the thief" - "I have sent it forth" - immediately; "and it shall enter the house of the thief" - this is one who steals his fellow's mind, that he has no claim against him, yet sues him and makes him swear; "and into the house of him who swears falsely by My Name" - literally; "and it shall lodge inside his house, and shall consume it, with its timber and its stones," and so on - from here you learn of things that fire and water do not destroy, but a false oath destroys them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:4: And further, we find that the sin of a false oath is equated with the desecration of the Name, as it is said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 9), "wild beasts come into the world because of a false oath and because of the desecration of the Name." And further we read in the Sifrei (Leviticus 19:12), "and you shall not swear falsely by My Name" - what does this teach? Since it is said (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God in vain," one might think one is liable only concerning the Explicit Name alone - from where do we include all the appellations? Scripture says "by My Name" - any name that is Mine. "And you shall profane the Name" - this teaches that a false oath is a desecration of the Name. And we read in Midrash Tanchuma, whoever betrays through oaths denies the Holy One, blessed be He, and has no forgiveness ever, as it is said (Exodus 20:7), "for [the LORD] will not hold guiltless" - to this point. And I have condensed his words to what is necessary for our purpose, so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:5: Further, we read in Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Matot), in these words, on (Numbers 30:3), "if a man vows a vow to the LORD" - this is what is written (Jeremiah 4:2), "and you shall swear, as the LORD lives, in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness" - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel, do not suppose that you are permitted to swear by My Name - even in truth you are not permitted to swear by My Name, unless all these qualities are in you: "you shall fear the LORD your God" - that you be like those called God-fearing, Abraham, Job, and Joseph - Abraham, as it is written (Genesis 22:12), "for now I know that you fear God"; Job, as it is written (Job 1:1), "a blameless and upright man, who feared God"; Joseph, as it is written (Genesis 42:18), "I fear God" - this is "you shall fear the LORD your God." "And Him shall you serve" - if you turn yourself to Torah and to occupy yourself with commandments and have no other service - therefore it says "and Him shall you serve." "And to Him shall you cleave" - but can a person cleave to the Shechinah? Has it not already been said (Deuteronomy 4:24), "for the LORD your God is a consuming fire"? Rather, this teaches you: whoever gives his daughter in marriage to a Torah scholar who reads and studies, does business for him, and benefits him from his possessions - concerning him it is said "and to Him shall you cleave." If you have all these qualities, you are permitted to swear, and if not, you are not permitted to swear. There was a story of King Yannai, who had two thousand towns, all of which were destroyed because of true oaths - how so? A person would say to his fellow, by an oath, I am going and shall eat such-and-such in such-and-such a place, and drink such-and-such in such-and-such a place, and they would go and fulfill their oaths, and [the towns] were destroyed - and if one who swears truly [causes such destruction], all the more so one who swears falsely - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:6: And on the verse "you shall not take" (Exodus 20:7), they explained in the Mechilta, in these words: "you shall not take" - why is this said? Because it says (Leviticus 19:12), "and you shall not swear falsely by My Name" - I know only that one should not swear falsely; from where do we know he should not accept upon himself to swear [falsely, i.e., accept a false oath from another]? Scripture says (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God" - before you accept upon yourself to swear, I am your God; once you accept upon yourself to swear [falsely], I am your Judge - as it is said, "for the LORD will not hold guiltless one who takes His Name in vain." It is impossible to say "will not hold guiltless," since it is already said (ibid. 34:7), "and He will hold guiltless" [in some readings]; and it is impossible to say "will hold guiltless," since it is already said "will not hold guiltless" - say from now: He holds guiltless those who repent, and does not hold guiltless those who do not repent - to this point, their wording.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:7: And by the plain meaning, "you shall not take" [lo tissa] is explained as meaning that a person should not accustom himself to bring up [lasat] the Name of Heaven with his mouth in vain, along the lines of (Psalms 16:4), "nor will I take up their names upon my lips" - and so Ramban, peace be upon him, explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:8: And in the Tikkunim (page 118a), concerning the severity of the sin of oaths, they said, in these words: but others, from whose mouths emerge breaths of an [false] oath, of them it is said (Proverbs 7:26), "for she has cast down many wounded" - and these are called "wounded," for they desecrate the Name of the LORD, and breaths emerge from their mouths - and likewise those whose speech is falsehood and swearing falsely, and mention His Name in vain and falsely - with that Name that emerges for vanity and falsehood, they build buildings that nullify them from the world - this is what is written (Jeremiah 2:30), "in vain have I struck your children" - woe to those people from whose mouths emerge false words and oaths - it were better for them not to have come into the world. All the colleagues rose and said, may the Merciful One save us, may the Merciful One save us - to this point, their wording. Also in the Zohar (Parashat Yitro, pages 87b, 91b), in explaining the verse, they elaborate on the severity of the sin, and we shall not copy its wording so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:9: And in Sefer Ta'amei HaMitzvot of the sage Rabbi Yitzchak ben Farchiya, peace be upon him, he explained, concerning the severity of the oath, in the commandment "you shall not take," in these words: "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God in vain" - for one who swears falsely cuts and separates the bridegroom from the bride - and this is "lo tissa" [you shall not lift/take], meaning: do not raise and elevate the LORD away from your God. And because one who swears falsely blemishes this seventh attribute [Malchut], therefore his punishment is so severe, "and shall consume its timber and its stones." And therefore it is juxtaposed with (Exodus 20:8), "remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" - for the Sabbath is the male, and one must sanctify it and not separate it, Heaven forfend. He further wrote, that one who swears is as though he takes hold of the precious object of the supernal covenant in his hand, and the proof is (Genesis 24:2), "put now your hand under my thigh" - and if, Heaven forfend, he swears in vain and falsely, he cuts and separates.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:10: Further, I heard in the name of the Kabbalists that in the verse "you shall not take" there are seventeen words, corresponding to the numerical value of "tov" [good], and to the numerical value of YHVH spelled out in full, and to the numerical value of "Torah," and to the numerical value of "seven" - to allude that one who swears falsely is uprooted from the good of the World to Come and from the rest mentioned, and from the sevenfold aspects alluded to in the oath [shevuah, related to sheva, seven] - for "shevuah" written defectively and vocalized totals sixty-six, the numerical value of Adonai plus the inclusive count.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:11: And included in the matter of the oath is being careful not to mention the Name of Heaven in vain, for whoever mentions it in vain is liable to excommunication (Nedarim 7b), and this is included in "you shall not take," as explained. And whoever is careful about this has a great reward in the World to Come, as it is written (Malachi 3:20), "but for you who fear My Name, the sun of righteousness shall rise" - and they explained in Nedarim (8b), these are people who fear to bring forth the Name of Heaven in vain - to this point. And the explanation of "the sun of righteousness" is explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 13.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:12: Also included in oaths is that one not extend his hand to his beard and swear, for this is [equivalent to] an oath - and so explained in the Idra of Naso (end of page 131a), in these words: and whoever extends his hand to his beard to swear is as one who swears by the thirteen adornments of the beard - to this point. Also, one should be careful not to swear "by truth," for YHVH is called "truth," as it is said (Jeremiah 10:10), "and the LORD, God, is truth." And likewise one should be careful not to swear "by my life," for the soul is a portion of God from above, and is found to be like swearing by the Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:13: Further, it is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 416, and siman 991) that one should not say "so may I merit the life of the World to Come" unless it is truly so. Further it is written there (siman 420) that in this era one should not swear to fulfill the commandments, for Satan will accuse and he will not fulfill his oath - and there is support for this from the teaching of Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Matot), which we copied above, saying (Deuteronomy 10:20), "you shall fear the LORD your God, Him you shall serve," and so on - if you have all these qualities, you may swear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:14: And concerning the sin of vows, they said in Tractate Nedarim (20a): it was taught, a person should never be accustomed to vows, for he shall eventually come to betray oaths. Further we read there (22a): the grandson of Rabbi Yannai the elder came before Rabbi Yannai the Great. He said to him, had you known that your record is opened and your deeds examined, would you have made a vow? And further he said, what did Rabban Gamliel open with, to that elder? "There is one who speaks rashly, like the piercings of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing" (Proverbs 12:18). Further there: whoever speaks rashly deserves to be pierced with a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing. Further there: it was taught, Rabbi Natan says, whoever vows is as though he built a high place [an illicit altar], and whoever fulfills it is as though he offered a sacrifice on it, and so on - and one who fulfills it without having his vow annulled [when he could] is as though he offered on that high place and is liable for slaughtering outside [the Temple].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:15: Further there, Shmuel said, whoever vows, even though he fulfills it, is called wicked. Rabbi Abahu said, what is the verse? "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall not be a sin in you" (Deuteronomy 23:23) - and he derives "cheder" from "cheder" [same root, "cease/refrain"]: it is written here, "but if you refrain from vowing," and it is written there (Job 3:17), "there the wicked cease [chadlu] from raging" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:16: And in chapter 10 (Nedarim 77b) we read: Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, taught, whoever vows, even though he fulfills it, is called a sinner. Rav Zevid said, what is the verse? "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall not be a sin in you" - implying that if you do not refrain, there is a sin - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:17: Further there, they said in Tractate Shabbat (32b): it was taught, Rabbi Natan says, because of the sin of vows, a man's wife dies, as it is said (Proverbs 22:27), "if you have nothing with which to pay, why should he take your bed from under you." Rabbi says, because of the sin of vows, children die while young, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 5:5), "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error; why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands" - and "the work of a person's hands" refers to his sons and daughters - to this point, relevant here. And the reason for this is because vows are in the supernal Mother, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna, and one must fulfill his vow and bring it to the place of action, which is the Shechinah - and if, Heaven forfend, he did not fulfill it, the sin is in the children and in the lower Mother, and therefore his wife dies.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:18: And in Midrash Kohelet (Rabbah 5:3) they explained this verse concerning those who pledge charity publicly and do not give. And incidentally we shall copy the severity of the sin of vows explained earlier there (Kohelet Rabbah 5:2), on the verse "it is better that you not vow," in these words: Rav Huna said, there was a story of one who vowed and did not pay, and set sail on the great sea, and his ship sank at sea and he died. Rabbi Shmuel said, whoever vows and does not pay causes his own wife to die, as it is written (Genesis 48:7), "and as for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died to me [alai]" - and so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach, page 175a), that Jacob was punished for a vow he did not fulfill, and this troubled Jacob more than all the distresses that passed over him - and from where do we know that it was because of Jacob? Because it is written "Rachel died to me [alai]" - "alai" certainly, because I delayed my vow - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:19: Further there, in the Midrash, Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, whoever vows and does not pay causes himself to come to transgression - idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed - and all are learned from Jacob: idolatry, as it is written (Genesis 35:2), "put away the foreign gods that are among you"; forbidden relations, as it is written, "for he had defiled Dinah their sister"; bloodshed, as it is written (ibid. 35:25), "and the two sons of Jacob took," and so on; and slander, as it is written (ibid. 31:1), "and he heard the words of Laban's sons." Rabbi Mana said, whoever vows and does not pay causes death to himself, as it is said (Deuteronomy 23:22), "for the LORD your God will surely require it of you." And Rabbi Ami said, there is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity - there is no death without sin, as it is said (Ezekiel 18:20), "the soul that sins, it shall die" - and no suffering without iniquity, as it is said (Psalms 89:33), "then I will visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with plagues."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:20: "Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" - Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse as referring to those who pledge charity publicly and do not give. "And do not say before the angel" - this is the cantor - "that it was an error" - let it be [regarded as] mine; "why should God be angry at your voice" - at that voice you spoke [in pledging]; "and destroy the work of your hands" - the diminishing of the commandments in that man's hand, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings a curse into them and destroys them from him - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:21: And in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Arachin) this teaching of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani is brought, that whoever vows and delays his vow eventually comes to idolatry, forbidden relations, bloodshed, and slander, and he proves all this from Jacob as stated in the teaching. However, it says there, Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, whoever vows and pays has a reward for the vowing and for the paying, as it is said (Psalms 76:12), "vow and pay to the LORD your God" - and whoever vows and delays his vow causes death to himself, as it is written (Deuteronomy 23:22), "for the LORD your God will surely require it of you" - from you, punishment is exacted, and not from your money. Rabbi Ami said, there is no death without sin - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:22: And it appears to me that the end of the verse, "and there shall be a sin in you," shall be understood along the lines explained in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 75b), "that He see no unseemly thing among you" (Deuteronomy 23:15), explained above (chapter 11), that the intent is that that sin is imprinted literally in his body - along these lines, "shall require it," which they explained, of blessed memory, as death, because speech makes a real happening within his very body, that the sin is marked upon him - and this is "and there shall be [vehayah] in you" - the sin itself in your very being - and therefore punishment is exacted from you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:23: And without doubt, what it says, that one who vows and pays has a reward for the vow and for the payment, refers to vows of commandments, or consecration, or Torah - and Scripture is precise about this, saying "to the LORD your God" - and further Scripture says "all around Him" [in the context of the fear surrounding Him] - for the vow or the oath is given only to one who fears Heaven, who is around the Holy One, blessed be He, along the lines of (Psalms 50:3), "and it is very tempestuous around Him" - which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Yevamot 121b), teaching that the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with the righteous to a hairsbreadth - and so it is proven from the teaching we copied above from Midrash Rabbah (Parashat Matot).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:24: Further, we read in Midrash Eichah (Rabbati 2:14), on the verse (Lamentations 2:10), "they sit on the ground" - Rabbi Elazar said, do not let the portion of vows be light in your eyes, for through the portion of vows the Great Sanhedrin of Zedekiah were killed, and so on - and the rest of the story, see there, so as not to be lengthy - and this same story is also brought in Nedarim (65a), with a slight difference between them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:25: And Rabbeinu Yaakov wrote (Yoreh De'ah, siman 203) that if they are pledging charity publicly and one must pledge with them, he should say "without a vow" - however, if it is a commandment incumbent on himself and obligatory upon him, such as one who says, I shall study this chapter, I shall study this tractate, and he fears lest he grow lax in the matter, though he has the ability to fulfill it, it is permitted for the vower to vow, to strengthen himself - for Rav Gidal said, from where do we know that one may swear to fulfill a commandment? As it is said (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to observe Your righteous judgments." And all the more so where he is accustomed to forgetting and transgressing one of the negative commandments, or is lax in fulfilling a positive commandment, it is permitted for him to vow and swear, to be strict with himself to keep and fulfill the commandments - and concerning this our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 13), "vows are a fence for abstinence." But from all other vows a person must distance himself greatly - to this point. And we have already written above that it is not fitting to swear and vow even to fulfill a commandment, unless the person is God-fearing enough that he will fulfill his vow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:26: And in Midrash Bereshit Rabbah, on the verse (Genesis 28:20), "and Jacob vowed a vow, saying," they explained that it is permitted, and even good, to vow in a time of distress, to perform a commandment and the like, in these words: "and Jacob vowed a vow, saying" - it is written (Psalms 66:14), "which my lips uttered, and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress" - Rabbi Yitzchak the Babylonian said, "and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress" - that he vowed a commandment at the time of his distress. What is "saying"? For [future] generations, so that they vow at the time of their distress. Jacob opened with a vow first, therefore whoever vows should attach the vow only to Him. Rabbi Abahu said, it is written (Psalms 132:2), "who swore to the LORD, vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob" - "to the Mighty One of Abraham" or "to the Mighty One of Isaac" is not written here, but "to the Mighty One of Jacob" - he attached the vow to the one who opened with it first - to this point. And nevertheless, it is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 403), that one who is in distress should not vow, but rather think and take counsel before there is a matter he can fulfill.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:27: And know that whoever vows to fulfill a commandment or to occupy himself with Torah for so many hours a day and the like, it is not fitting to have his vow annulled unless he shows the court that it is a great compulsion - and if they annul it for him and there was no great compulsion in the matter, Heaven does not annul it for him - and this is what they were precise about, of blessed memory, in saying (Nedarim 8a), "a great vow he vowed to the God of Israel" - that the Holy One, blessed be He, should say, what wrong did you find in Me, that you have distanced yourself from Me? And it is like the parable of a man who says to a king of flesh and blood, by your head, my lord, on such-and-such a day I shall bring you such-and-such a gift - that if he does not bring it, his head becomes forfeit to the king, unless the king knows he was prevented by circumstances beyond his control. And the matter of occupying oneself with Torah or a commandment is literally a gift to the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and whoever is lenient and annuls his vow is lenient with the honor of the King of the universe. And this is unlike annulling one's own personal vows, such as that he will or will not eat [something], where it is a commandment that he have his vow annulled, since there is no commandment involved in the matter.
